blocks.p: Dear Stephen, today I remembered a wedding. Your cousin’s, in the old stone church on the hill, with the roof leaking over the third row of folding chairs and everyone shuffling along to keep dry. They promised each other “till death,” out loud, in front of everybody, and nobody thought it was a strange thing to promise. Mom sang, badly. You cried. If you ever get the chance to say it to anyone, say it slowly.
Lyda Thorne read the Gospels the way she read a ledger: once quickly, for the shape, and then slowly, looking for the place where the numbers did not add up.

She read them at night, in the counting house above the Thorne pier on Philippa, after the last of the day’s manifests were signed. Sol knew because he could see her lamp from the window of his room across the yard, a small square of yellow high up in the dark bulk of the warehouse, burning past the middle of the night. She had taken the grey notebook from him on the ramp of the Kestrel and had not given it back, and she would not let him near it. When he came up the counting-house stair the first week with a pot of tea and an offer, she met him at the top of it.
“No,” she said. “Thank you for the tea.”
“I only thought, if there were places that were hard...”

“There are. I’m finding them.” She took the pot out of his hands. “Sol. I’ve heard you read this thing aloud in the loft for more than a year, and heard about the dozen other rooms. People cry at it. They fall down in front of it and go into rivers over it. If I get anywhere, I want to have got there by myself. Not because you explained it well. You explain everything well. You were a bishop.” She did not say it unkindly. “Go to bed.”
He went. It was the hardest thing he had done since Viper.

She did not take her questions to him. She took them to Lucan, which Sol understood, and which hurt him a little, and which he did not let himself mind. The two of them would sit at the end of the pier in the evenings with their collars up against the wind off the estuary, the doctor with his little book and Lyda with the ledger she had begun to keep, a thin one bound in Thorne green, in which she wrote her objections in a hard small hand and drew a line through them when they were answered. Sol saw the ledger once, left open on the counting-house table. Most of the lines were not drawn through. Some had a second line written underneath in a different pencil, as if she had come back later and argued with herself.
He heard some of it anyway. Philippa’s port town was small, and voices carried over water.
“They don’t agree,” she said to Lucan one evening. “Four accounts of the same morning. One angel at the tomb, or two. Sitting, or standing. Women going at dawn, or while it was still dark.”
“Does that trouble you?”

“No. That’s what bothers me.” The wind took some of it. “If four of my clerks gave me the same figures to the last decimal, I’d know they had copied each other. These didn’t copy each other. They were all standing in different places, and they all got the main number the same.”

And another night, with a short hard laugh: “And they’re stupid. The friends. They’re stupid and frightened all the way through. They fall asleep. They run. The big one swears he never met him. Nobody writing a lie makes their own people look that bad.” A pause. “And when the women come back and say the grave’s empty, nobody believes them. The first people to know, and nobody believes them.” The laugh again, but differently. “I know that one.”
“That is not faith,” Lucan said, in the dry voice he used for diagnoses. “That is bookkeeping.”
“I know,” Lyda said. “I’m not there. I’m only telling you the books balance better than I thought.”

She was not there at the turn of the year. Sol prayed for her every night, and every night he made himself ask for nothing but that whatever came to her would be true, and not for him. It was a hard prayer. He was not always sure he meant it.

Then, four months after Viper, he came up the counting-house stair late at night for no reason except that her lamp was out, and it had never been out before the middle of the night, and he was afraid.

She was sitting in the dark by the window with the notebook closed on her knees. The lamp was out because she had let it burn out, and had not got up. The light of the port came in through the glass, the cranes and the berths and the long reflections on the black water, and he could see her face by it. It was wet.
“Sit down,” she said. “Don’t say anything yet.”
He sat on a crate of manifests across from her.

“When I was dead,” she said. “On the deck. Lucan says nine minutes.” She turned the notebook over in her hands. “I’ve never told you what it was like. You never asked. I think you were afraid to.” She looked at the window. “There was nothing. Not dark. Dark is something. Nothing. I always thought that’s what there was. When I was a girl and the church people came round with their Pearls and their City of the Throne, and I didn’t have a Halo, so none of it was for me anyway, I used to lie awake and think: well, then, nothing. That’s what I get. And on the deck I found out I was right.” She was quiet a moment. “And then I came back, and the first thing in the world was your voice. Counting. And saying his name between the numbers, like you were hammering on a door.”
“Lyda...”

“I said don’t.” She opened the notebook. She did not need the lamp; she knew where it was. “There’s a man at the end of the fourth one. One of the friends. He wasn’t there the first time, when the others saw him. They tell him, and he says no. He says, unless I see the marks of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the marks, and put my hand into his side, I won’t believe it. I won’t.” Her voice was steady and very low. “I’ve been that man my whole life, Sol. I’ve been that man about everything. About the church. About you. About whether a ship will come home. I don’t believe anything I can’t put my hand on.”
“I know.”

“So I waited for him to get told off. That’s what happens in the Book of Life, when you doubt. You get gently corrected.” She laughed, wetly. “He came back. A week later. The doors were locked, and he came back, and he walked straight over to that one man, the one who wouldn’t, and held out his hands. Put your finger here, and see my hands. Put out your hand and place it in my side. He came back for the one who said no.” She closed the book on her finger. “And then he says the other thing. Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”
Sol did not trust himself to speak.

“When you were baptized, the hum stopped,” Lyda said. “You told me. Teo said the same. Tobin. Everybody in every one of those rooms has a story about the quiet. It’s how they know.” She touched the place behind her left ear where Lucan’s implant sat under the skin, a thing that had never spoken to Sion and never would. “I’ve got nothing to go quiet. Lucan’s box doesn’t talk to anybody. When I come up out of the water, nothing will happen. Nobody will be able to see a thing. Not you, not me. There won’t be any sign at all.”
“Lucan’s drum would,” Sol said.

“Then Imre doesn’t get his cups on me. Not ever.” She wiped her face with the heel of her hand. “It’ll be mine.” She looked at him straight. “And not yours. I’m not doing this so you can marry a believer, and I’m not doing it because you cried over me on a deck. If you ever once think that I did, I’ll know, and I’ll never forgive you. Do you understand?”
“Yes.”
“I’m going to ask Teo,” she said. “Not you. Not Tobin. Teo.”

They went down to the river at first light, a week later, with the small church of Philippa trailing behind them along the bank: dockhands and clerks and a baker and his wife and the two widows who kept the chandlery, perhaps twenty people in their coats, their breath smoking in the cold. The Wend went by brown and slow among the reeds above the cranes. There was a place where the bank shelved gently, and where the church had been taking people down into the water since Sol’s first summer there, and the reeds had been trodden flat in a little path.

Teo was shaking. He stood up to his waist in the current in his shirt with his teeth chattering, and Sol did not think it was all the cold. He had baptized others before. He had never baptized anyone who had carried him on her hip.

Lyda waded out to him without looking back. She stood in front of her brother in the brown water, and said something to him too low for the bank to hear, and Teo nodded, and put one hand behind her shoulders and the other over her folded hands, the way Tobin had taught him.
“In the name of the Father,” Teo said. His voice cracked and steadied. “And of the Son. And of the Holy Spirit.”

She went under. The river closed over her. For a moment there was only the brown water running, and the reeds, and the cranes standing against the white sky downriver, and Sol on the bank with his heart hammering as hard as it had on the deck of the Petrel.
She came up.

Nothing happened. She stood in the current with her hair streaming and the water running off her face, and she put her hand up behind her ear, and nothing happened at all. No hum stopped. No lights went out. She looked at the bank, and at her brother, and at the sky.
Then she began to laugh.

Sol had never heard her laugh like that. None of them had. It came up out of her from somewhere deep, helpless and wet and astonished, and it went on, and in the middle of it it turned without any warning into weeping, and then back, so that she stood in the river doing both at once with her hands over her face, and Teo, who had no idea what to do, put his arms around her and held on, and the two of them stood there in the current, and the little church on the bank, who had seen a good many people go into that river, had never seen anyone come out of it like that, and began, one by one, to laugh too.
They were married a month later, in the loft above the Thorne warehouse, where the church of Philippa met.

Sol shaved that morning in front of a small square of mirror in his room across the yard. The face in it was not the smooth one he had worn for four hundred years. This one was grey all through, with two deep lines from the nose to the corners of the mouth and a looseness beginning under the jaw, and it came on now at the ordinary pace, a day at a time, like everyone’s had once. It was the face of a man of fifty-two who would be fifty-three, and then sixty, and then, if he was given them, eighty.

You could still go back, the voice said, quietly, as he wiped the blade. Fall away a little. Only a little. It comes back on, you know it does, it happens all the time out here. They would renew you. Forty again. She could have a Halo; they’d give her one. Forever. The two of you, forever.
Sol rinsed the blade. “Christ,” he said to the mirror, mildly, as a man declines a second helping, and the voice went out like a blown match, and he finished shaving.

In the inner colonies people married for a term: a century, usually, renewable at the end of it by both parties, and the church blessed the term and recorded the Renewal, and when it lapsed there were no hard feelings, because there were no hard feelings about anything. Sol had blessed hundreds of them. He had never once heard anyone promise what Tobin asked him to promise in the loft that afternoon, with the late light coming slantwise through the cargo doors and forty people crowded onto crates and coils of rope.

Tobin read first, from the grey notebook, holding it in his huge hands as if it were a bird. He read it slowly, the way he read everything. Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death. Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it. Then he closed the book and looked at the two of them, and his eyes were already wet, and he did not care.

“I’ve never done this one,” he said. “Stephen didn’t teach me. Lucan found the words in an old record. So bear with me.” He cleared his throat. “Sol. Will you have her, and keep her, in sickness and in health, for richer or poorer, as long as you both shall live? Till death parts you?”

Till death. The words went into Sol the way a word had once gone into him in a market, and stayed, like a splinter. No one in Sion had said them since the Tragedy. They were not even forbidden. They were simply gone, the way rain was gone, and the leaking roof over the third row of folding chairs.
“Till death parts us,” Sol said. “Yes. Gladly.”

Lyda did not wait for Tobin to ask her. She had her own words, and she said them looking straight at Sol, in her flat practical voice, as if she were reading out the terms of a contract she had gone over line by line and meant to keep. He knew where she had found them. It was a short book, about a widow who would not go home.

“Where you go, I will go,” she said. “Where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried.” She paused. “That one’s the part I like. Everybody out here’s going to die anyway. I’d just as soon do it next to you.”
The loft laughed. Tobin wept. Lucan, on a coil of rope by the window, wrote in his little book and did not look up for a long time.

There was bread afterward, and a cheap Philippan wine that tasted of the barrels it had been shipped in, and Teo played Ina Moss’s tin whistle, badly, until someone took it from him and played it well. The baker’s wife danced with Lucan, who turned out to know how. The widows from the chandlery danced with each other. Sol danced with his wife on the rough boards of the loft, slowly, because his knees would not let him do it any other way, and she did not seem to mind. When the light had gone from the cargo doors they walked home along the pier together in the beginning of a rain, with her hand in the crook of his arm, and he opened the door of the house across the yard for her, and they went in, and he closed it.

Some time in the night the rain found a seam in the roof and began to come through over the end of the table, a drop at a time, onto the boards. Sol lay in the dark with his wife asleep beside him and listened to it keep time. For four hundred years he had lived without a clock that could run out. He did not get up to stop it.
